# Agriculture Infrastructure Fund: Subsidies, Loans and Application Guide

27 June 202610 min read

Key takeaways

* The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund provides medium to long term debt financing for post-harvest management projects.
* Loans under the scheme qualify for a three percent interest subvention per year for up to seven years.
* Credit guarantee coverage is available under the CGTMSE scheme for loans up to two crore rupees without collateral.
* Eligible projects include cold storage units, warehouses, sorting facilities, and primary processing centres.
* Farmers, FPOs, start-ups, and cooperatives can apply online through the official portal with a project report.

Many farmers in India face heavy losses because they lack facilities to store and process their harvest. When crop prices drop in the market, they are forced to sell their produce at low rates because they cannot store it safely. To address this gap, the central government created the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, also known as the AIF scheme. This initiative provides affordable loans with interest subsidies to build post-harvest management and community farming assets. This guide explains how you can use this fund to build storage facilities and add value to your crops.

## What is the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund?

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund is a medium to long term debt financing facility set up by the central government. Under this scheme, the government provides financial support to build post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets. The fund aims to reduce post-harvest losses, which currently waste a significant portion of India's crop output. By providing cheaper loans, the government hopes to attract private investment into rural areas, creating jobs and strengthening the local economy.

The scheme runs for a period of ten years, from the financial year twenty-twenty to twenty-thirty. It offers benefits like interest subvention and credit guarantees to make borrowing safer and cheaper for rural entrepreneurs. Banks and financial institutions provide the loans, while the government monitors the applications and pays the interest subsidies. This scheme allows farmers to store their crops and sell them when market prices are favourable, increasing overall profits.

## Who is eligible to apply for the AIF scheme?

A wide range of individuals and organisations can apply for loans under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund. Individual farmers, joint liability groups, and self-help groups are eligible to receive funding. Farmer Producer Organisations, commonly known as FPOs, and agricultural cooperative societies are also encouraged to apply. By supporting collective groups, the scheme helps small farmers pool their resources and build shared facilities that they could not afford individually.

Private agri-entrepreneurs, start-ups, and central or state government agencies are eligible to apply under the scheme rules. This broad eligibility ensures that anyone who wants to build agricultural infrastructure can access these benefits. Even local panchayats and municipal bodies can apply to create community assets like rural markets or sorting yards. The diversity of eligible applicants helps build a comprehensive supply chain from farms to retail markets in cities.

## Eligible projects under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

The scheme focuses primarily on projects that help manage crops after harvest and prepare them for sale. You can get a loan to build cold storage units, warehouses, silos, and cold chains. These facilities keep perishable crops fresh for longer periods, reducing wastage and distress sales. You can also build pack houses, sorting and grading units, and primary processing centres that clean and pack the produce.

The fund also supports community farming assets like organic input production units, bio-stimulant manufacturing, and precision farming equipment. You can get loans for customized hiring centres that rent out tractors and implements to local farmers. The scheme also funds projects that use internet-of-things devices or sensors to monitor crop storage conditions. Any infrastructure that directly benefits farmers by reducing costs or adding value is eligible.

## Understanding the interest subvention benefit

The most attractive feature of the AIF scheme is the three percent interest subvention per year on loans. This means the government pays three percent of your loan interest rate, reducing your out-of-pocket interest expense. For example, if a bank offers you an infrastructure loan at nine percent, the subvention reduces your actual interest rate to six percent. This benefit makes borrowing highly affordable for rural projects.

This interest subvention is available for a maximum period of seven years on loans up to two crore rupees. If you take a larger loan, the subvention still applies, but only to the first two crore rupees of the principal. The subvention amount is credited directly to your loan account by the government, ensuring a smooth process. This subsidy reduces the financial pressure on new projects during their initial years of operation.

## Credit guarantee coverage under the CGTMSE scheme

Many small entrepreneurs and FPOs struggle to get bank loans because they do not have land or buildings to offer as collateral. To solve this problem, the AIF scheme provides credit guarantee coverage through the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises, or CGTMSE. The government covers the fee for this guarantee, making it free for the borrower. This coverage encourages banks to approve loans without demanding extra security.

This credit guarantee is available for loans up to two crore rupees. If the borrower fails to repay the loan due to business failure, the guarantee fund pays the bank up to eighty-five percent of the outstanding amount. This coverage significantly reduces the risk for lending banks, making them more willing to support rural projects. It is a critical feature that helps landless entrepreneurs and FPOs obtain capital.

## How to prepare a project report for AIF approval

To apply for the loan, you must submit a detailed project report, also known as a DPR. The report must explain the type of infrastructure you want to build, its location, and the total cost. You need to include details of the machinery, construction materials, and other capital expenses. The report must also show the projected income and expenditure for the next seven to ten years.

Banks review the project report to check if the business is viable and if you can repay the loan from the earnings. You can hire a professional consultant or use online templates provided on the AIF portal to prepare this document. Make sure your figures are realistic and based on local market rates for construction and machinery. A well-prepared report increases your chances of getting quick bank approval.

## Step by step online application process for AIF

The application process is handled online through a dedicated portal to ensure transparency and speed. First, you must register as a beneficiary on the portal using your mobile number and Aadhaar. After registration, fill in the online application form with your personal details, land details, and project details. You must upload your project report, land documents, and identity proof on the website.

Once you submit the form, the AIF team reviews your project for eligibility under the scheme rules. If approved, your application is sent to your selected bank for credit appraisal. The bank will review your credit history, verify your documents, and sanction the loan if they find it suitable. The online system allows you to select which bank branch you want to work with.

## Documents required for the AIF loan application

Having your documents ready helps avoid delays in the application and verification process. You will need standard KYC documents, including your Aadhaar card, PAN card, and registered mobile number. You must also provide land ownership documents or lease agreements for the project site, proving you have legal possession. A detailed project report and quotations for machinery are also mandatory.

For FPOs and cooperative societies, you must submit registration certificates, audit reports for the last three years, and board resolutions authorizing the loan. You also need to provide bank account statements and details of existing loans if any. The lending bank might ask for additional documents like tax returns or local authority permissions depending on the size of the project. Ensure all copies are clear. Keep digital copies of all files on your phone so you can resubmit them quickly if the bank requests them.

## Interest rates and repayment terms for AIF loans

The government has capped the interest rates that banks can charge under this scheme to protect borrowers. The interest rate is limited to a maximum of nine percent per year for loans that qualify for subvention. With the three percent subvention applied, your effective interest rate is capped at six percent, which is much lower than regular commercial rates. This cap prevents banks from charging high rates.

The repayment period for these loans is flexible and can extend up to seven years, including a moratorium period. The moratorium period is a temporary holiday during which you do not have to pay the principal amount. This period can range from six months to two years, giving you time to build the facility and start earning. It is a helpful feature that protects cash flow during construction. A longer repayment term helps you manage seasonal cash flows without default risk.

## Role of FPOs and cooperatives in infrastructure building

Farmer Producer Organisations and cooperatives are crucial for the success of this scheme. Since individual small farmers have limited produce, they cannot justify the cost of running a large warehouse or cold storage. FPOs can pool the produce of hundreds of members, making it viable to build and operate processing facilities. This collective approach helps smallholders get better prices by negotiating directly with large buyers.

The scheme provides special benefits to cooperative groups, including priority processing of applications and higher borrowing limits. By building shared infrastructure, cooperatives help reduce transit losses and lower transportation costs for member farmers. They can also buy inputs in bulk and store them in their warehouses, distributing them to members at cheaper rates. This strengthens the rural cooperative network. This collective strength is the way to get better terms in the market.

## Common reasons for AIF loan application rejection

Understanding why applications get rejected helps you prepare a better application. A common reason for rejection is submitting an incomplete project report with unrealistic financial projections. If the bank finds that your projected income is too low to cover the loan instalments, they will reject the file. Another issue is poor credit scores or pending defaults on past loans by the applicants.

Incomplete land documents or lack of clear title to the project site also lead to quick rejection. If the land is agricultural, you may need a conversion certificate to build commercial warehouses depending on state laws. Failing to provide quotations for machinery or using unverified suppliers can also cause problems. You should address these points before submitting your final application. You should verify that your land title is clear and free from any disputes before filing the papers.

## How to track your AIF application status online

After submitting your application, you can track its progress by logging into the AIF portal. The dashboard shows the current stage of your file, such as pending with ministry, sent to bank, or sanctioned. You will also receive SMS updates on your registered mobile number when the status changes. This transparency prevents you from having to visit bank offices for updates.

If the portal shows that the bank has raised a query, you must respond quickly to prevent rejection. You can upload the requested documents directly on the website to resolve the query. If your application is delayed at any stage, you can use the grievance cell on the portal to request a review. Tracking your application online keeps you informed throughout the process.

## How AIF benefits start-ups and rural youth

The scheme offers exciting opportunities for rural youth and agri-graduates to start their own businesses. Instead of moving to cities for low-paying jobs, young people can set up sorting, grading, or custom hiring centres in their villages. The low interest rates and lack of collateral requirements make it easier for young entrepreneurs to secure bank loans. This self-employment path helps retain talent in rural areas.

Agri-tech start-ups can also use the fund to build cold chains or deploy smart sensors in local warehouses. The government provides additional mentorship and networking support to AIF-funded start-ups through agricultural universities. By using modern technology, these start-ups help local farmers reduce wastage and find premium buyers. This business model creates a win-win situation for both youth and farmers.

## Monitoring and implementation of the AIF scheme

The central government has set up monitoring committees at the national, state, and district levels to ensure the success of the fund. These committees review the progress of sanctioned loans and ensure that the interest subvention is paid on time. They also work to resolve bottleneck issues between borrowers and banks. This multi-level monitoring ensures that the scheme benefits reach the grassroots level.

The district-level committee, headed by the district collector, meets regularly to review local applications and coordinate with regional banks. Farmers can approach these committees if they face unfair delays or difficulties in getting their loans processed. The active involvement of local administration helps speed up approvals and ensures that the infrastructure projects are completed on schedule. This governance structure ensures public funds are used effectively.

## Frequently asked questions

What is the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund?
:   The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund is a government scheme providing debt financing with interest subsidies to build post-harvest management and community farming assets.

How much interest subsidy do I get under AIF?
:   You get a three percent interest subvention per year on your loan, which directly reduces the interest rate charged by the bank.

What is the maximum loan amount eligible for subvention?
:   The interest subvention is available for loans up to two crore rupees. For loans exceeding this amount, the subsidy is limited to the first two crore rupees.

For how many years can I receive the interest subvention?
:   The interest subvention benefit is available for a maximum period of seven years from the date of loan disbursement.

Is there a credit guarantee for AIF loans?
:   Yes, the government provides credit guarantee coverage under the CGTMSE scheme for loans up to two crore rupees without requiring collateral.

Who pays the fee for the credit guarantee?
:   The central government covers the credit guarantee fee under the AIF scheme, so the borrower does not have to pay anything extra for this protection.

Can individual farmers apply for AIF loans?
:   Yes, individual farmers, joint liability groups, and self-help groups are fully eligible to apply for loans under this infrastructure scheme.

Are FPOs eligible to apply under the AIF scheme?
:   Yes, Farmer Producer Organisations and primary agricultural cooperative societies are eligible and receive priority processing for building shared facilities.

Can I build a warehouse using AIF funding?
:   Yes, warehouses, cold storage units, silos, and pack houses are all eligible post-harvest management projects under this fund.

What are community farming assets under AIF?
:   These include projects like custom hiring centres, organic input production units, bio-stimulant plants, and precision farming equipment sharing centres.

How do I apply for the AIF scheme?
:   You must apply online through the official Agriculture Infrastructure Fund portal by registering your details and uploading your project report.

What is a DPR in the AIF application?
:   A DPR stands for Detailed Project Report, which outlines the project costs, machinery details, location, and projected financial returns of your business.

Is there a limit on bank interest rates under AIF?
:   Yes, the interest rate charged by banks under this scheme is capped at a maximum of nine percent per year for loans eligible for subvention.

What is the moratorium period for AIF loans?
:   The moratorium is a repayment holiday during construction, ranging from six months to two years, where you do not have to pay the principal.

Can a start-up apply for AIF funding?
:   Yes, agriculture start-ups and private entrepreneurs are eligible to apply for loans to build innovative storage and cold chain solutions.

# Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) from MOA

  

Indian Government has recently launched a new Scheme of financing facility under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) of Rs. 1 Lakh Crore. The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund is a medium – long term debt financing facility for investment in projects for post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets through interest subvention and credit guarantee. The scheme will support Agri-entrepreneurs, Farmer Producer Organization (FPO), and Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS). Under the scheme, bank and the financial institution will provide Rs. 1 Lakh Crore as loans with interest subvention of 3% per annum and credit guarantee coverage under CGTMSE scheme for loans up to Rs. 2 Crore. The present article briefs the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme.

##### Objectives of Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

The key objective of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) is to provide financial support for agriculture entrepreneurs to improve agriculture infrastructure in the country.

##### Benefits of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)

The beneficiaries of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme will include:

* Farmers
* SHG – a self-help group
* Agri-entrepreneurs
* Startups
* Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS)
* Marketing Cooperative Societies
* Farmer Producer Organization (FPO
* Joint Liability Groups (JLG)

![agri marketing infrastructure scheme](assets/images/industrial-subsidies/Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) from MOA, Subsidy Consultants.jpg)

* Multipurpose Cooperative Societies
* Central/State agency or local Body sponsored Public-Private Partnership Projects

##### Benefits of Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

This financing facility will have numerous benefits for all the stakeholders in the agriculture eco-system:

Benefits to Farmers FPOs, PACS & Marketing Cooperative Societies

* AIF will improve the overall income of farmers
* The Improved marketing infrastructure will farmers to sell directly to a larger base of consumers and hence, increase value realization for the farmers
* AIF will make farmers independent and improve access to market
* Farmers can be able to decide when to sell in the market and improve realization using the modern packaging and cold storage system access.
* Benefits to Agri entrepreneurs and start-ups
* With a dedicated source of funding, entrepreneurs will push for innovation in the agriculture sector by leveraging new-age technologies including IoT (internet of things), AI (artificial intelligence), etc.
* AIF will improve avenues for collaboration between entrepreneurs and farmers.

##### Duration of the scheme

The duration of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund scheme shall be from the current financial year to the Financial year 2029 (10 years).

Financial Assistance under Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)

Under the scheme, banks and financial institutions will provide Rs. 1 Lakh Crore as loans with interest subvention of 3% per annum and credit guarantee coverage under CGTMSE scheme for loans up to Rs. 2 Crore.

##### Interest Subvention Cost

All loans under AIF will have an interest subvention of 3% per annum up to a limit of Rs. 2 crores.

This subvention will be available for a maximum period of 7 years. In the case of loans beyond Rs.2 crore, then interest subvention will be limited up to 2 crores.

The loans will be disbursed in four years starting with the sanction of Rs. 10,000 crores in the current financial year and Rs. 30,000 crore each in the next three fiscal years.

The extent and percentage of funding to private entrepreneurs out of the total financing facility may be fixed by the National Monitoring Committee.

##### Credit Guarantee Cost

Credit guarantee coverage will be available for eligible borrowers from the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) under Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme for a loan up to Rs. 2 crores. The Government will pay the fee for AIF coverage

##### Moratorium for Repayment

The moratorium for repayment under this AIF may vary subject to a minimum of 6 months and a maximum of 2 years.

##### Eligible Projects

The scheme will facilitate setting up and modernization of key elements of the following projects:

* Post-Harvest Management Projects
* Viable projects for building community farming assets

  

![Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure Scheme](assets/images/about/aif-1.jpg)  
 ![agri marketing infrastructure scheme](assets/images/about/aif-2.jpg)  
 ![Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure Scheme](assets/images/about/aif-3.jpg)

##### Criteria for selection of Eligible Borrower

Lending institutions will decide criteria for selection of eligible borrower in consultation with National Bank for Agriculture & Rural Development and monitoring committees:

All scheduled commercial banks scheduled cooperative banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), Small Finance Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), and National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) will provide this financing facility, after signing of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with NABARD.

##### AIF specific focus

As part of this scheme, the Government will give specific focus to SC/ST entrepreneurs and women entrepreneurs. 24% of total grants – in – aid under the scheme should be utilized for SC/ST entrepreneurs (16% for SC and 8% for ST). Besides this, lending institutions will ensure adequate coverage of entrepreneurs belonging to women and other weaker segments of society. It has to be ensured that the benefits of the scheme are inclusive and accrue to the intended beneficiaries.

##### Management of AIF

Agri Infra fund will be managed and monitored through an online Management Information System (MIS) platform. Using this portal, all qualified entities can apply for loans under the fund. The platform will provide benefits such as transparency of interest rates offered by multiple banks, scheme details including interest subvention and credit guarantee offered, minimum documentation, faster approval process as also integration with other scheme benefits.

The **[Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)](https://agriinfra.dac.gov.in/)** also supports **[greenfield projects](https://msmeloans.in/greenfield-projects/)**, which involve the development of new agricultural infrastructure from the ground up. Entrepreneurs, farmer producer organizations (FPOs), agri-startups, and cooperatives can establish new facilities such as warehouses, cold storage units, processing centers, and logistics infrastructure with financial support under the scheme.

Greenfield agricultural infrastructure projects help improve post-harvest management, reduce wastage of perishable products, and strengthen the agricultural supply chain. Through the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, eligible businesses can obtain loans with interest subsidy benefits and credit guarantee support to develop modern agricultural infrastructure including cold storage facilities, supply chain logistics, and food processing units.

Interest Rate under Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

#### Example

If a cold storage project takes a loan of **₹2 crore** at an interest rate of **10%**, the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund provides a subsidy of **3%**. The borrower effectively pays only **7% interest**. This reduces the interest burden by approximately **₹6 lakh per year**.

# Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) Explained: India's ₹1 Lakh Crore Scheme That Is Rebuilding Farming From the Ground Up

![Euroasia Aquatic Private Limited]()

### Euroasia Aquatic Private Limited

#### Making Compliance Effortless. Your single partner for Start-up Certification, Tax, Tenders, & Digital Growth.

By Euroasia Aquatic Private Limited | Agri-Business Advisory · Government Scheme Consulting · MSME Funding · Ahmedabad, India

The Problem Nobody Talks About at the Farm Gate

India produces enough food to feed itself and a significant portion of the world. We are among the top global producers of fruits, vegetables, milk, spices, and cereals. Our farmers work hard, our land is fertile, and our agricultural output grows year after year.

And yet, somewhere between the farm and the consumer, we lose nearly ₹92,000 crore worth of food every single year.

Not because of drought. Not because of bad seeds. Not because of poor farming.

Because of what happens - or more accurately, what doesn't happen - after the crop is harvested.

The cold storage isn't there. The warehouse isn't built. The processing unit doesn't exist in that district. The sorting and grading facility is 200 kilometres away. So the tomatoes rot in the field. The onions go bad in the open air. The grain gets damaged in inadequate storage. And the farmer who spent six months growing the crop watches its value collapse before it ever reaches a buyer who would pay a fair price.

This is not a farming problem. It is an infrastructure problem.

And the Government of India announced a ₹1 lakh crore solution for it in 2020.

It is called the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) - officially known as the National Agriculture Infra Financing Facility - and it is one of the most significant and least understood agricultural financing schemes in the country today.

What Is the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund? The Complete Explanation

Origin and Purpose

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) was announced by the Finance Minister on May 15, 2020, as part of the Aatmanirbhar Bharat economic package. It is a Central Sector Scheme formulated by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare (DA&FW) under the Ministry of Agriculture.

The core purpose is straightforward but transformational: provide medium to long-term debt financing for viable projects related to post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets - at the farm gate, at aggregation points, and across the agricultural value chain.

In plain language: the government created a structured financing mechanism to make it financially feasible for farmers, agri-entrepreneurs, FPOs, cooperatives, and startups to build the infrastructure that India's agriculture so desperately needs.

The scheme operates from 2020–21 to 2032–33, with loan disbursements completing by the end of FY 2025–26. Total financing facility: ₹1,00,000 crore.

The Three Pillars of AIF Support

1. Interest Subvention All loans under AIF carry a 3% per annum interest subvention - a direct reduction in the interest rate you pay on your loan. This subvention applies to loans up to ₹2 crore per project per location, for a maximum period of 7 years. The lending rate is capped, ensuring the benefit actually reaches the borrower.

For loans above ₹2 crore, the subvention is still applicable but limited to the ₹2 crore component.

2. Credit Guarantee For loans up to ₹2 crore, credit guarantee coverage is available under the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme - and the government pays the fee for this coverage. This removes the collateral barrier for smaller projects.

For FPOs (Farmer Producer Organisations), additional credit guarantee coverage is available through NABSanrakshan Trustee Company Pvt. Ltd., further strengthening financial security.

3. Convergence with Other Schemes AIF projects can be structured alongside other central or state government schemes. If capital subsidy support is available under another programme, it can count toward the promoter's contribution - lowering the upfront investment required and improving overall project viability.

The Scale of What Has Already Happened

The numbers reflect a scheme that is working:

1,73,298 registered beneficiaries on the portal

1,54,397 applications submitted

₹72,178 crore loan amount from received applications

₹47,575 crore sanctioned for 74,508 projects (as of August 2024)

₹78,596 crore in total investment mobilised in the agriculture sector

35 States and UTs covered

In FY 2024–25, ₹18,539 lakh was released under convergent schemes, benefiting over 2,69,200 farmers.

Who Is Eligible for the AIF Scheme?

The scheme is deliberately broad in its eligibility - recognising that agricultural infrastructure creation cannot be left to any single category of actor.

Eligible entities include:

Individual farmers and agriculturists

Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs)

Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies (PACS)

Self Help Groups (SHGs)

Agri-entrepreneurs, startups, and private companies in agriculture

Agricultural marketing cooperatives

Multi-Purpose Cooperative Societies (MPCS)

APMCs (Agricultural Produce Market Committees) - added in the 2021 expansion

State agencies, national and state federations of cooperatives

Federations of FPOs and federations of SHGs

Central/State agency or Local Body sponsored Public-Private Partnership projects

Key structure rules:

One eligible entity can set up projects in different locations - all eligible for loans up to ₹2 crore per location

Private sector entities (farmers, agri-entrepreneurs, startups) can avail benefits for a maximum of 25 projects

The 25-project limit does not apply to state agencies, national/state federations of cooperatives, and federations of FPOs or SHGs

Multiple participating lending institutions: Commercial Banks, Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), Small Finance Banks, NCDC, NBFCs, and more - giving applicants genuine choice in their lending partner.

What Projects Are Funded Under AIF?

AIF covers a wide range of post-harvest and farm-gate infrastructure. Eligible projects include:

Post-Harvest Management Infrastructure:

Cold storage chains and cold rooms

Warehouses and silos

Pack houses and assaying units

Sorting and grading units

Processing units (primary processing integrated with secondary)

Logistics and transport infrastructure

Community Farming Assets:

Organic input production facilities

Smart and precision agriculture infrastructure

Supply chain services for cluster-based farming

Recent 2024 Additions (Cabinet Expansion):

Viable projects for community farming infrastructure

Integrated primary and secondary processing projects (as a single unit)

Solar projects under PM-KUSUM Component-A - for FPOs, cooperatives, and panchayats - bringing clean energy convergence into the agricultural infrastructure framework

Before AIF: The Hidden Infrastructure Crisis That Was Bleeding Agriculture

To understand what AIF changes, you have to understand what the landscape looked like - and for many areas still looks like - without it.

Post-Harvest Losses Were Eating the Farm Economy

India's post-harvest losses were not a secret. Studies had documented them for decades. Farmers knew it intuitively - they had watched their produce degrade, their prices collapse at the mandi, their income reduced to a fraction of what it could have been with proper storage and processing.

A potato farmer in Uttar Pradesh grows a bumper crop. But there is no cold storage in his block. He is forced to sell everything within days of harvest - exactly when every other farmer in the region is also selling - driving prices down to levels that barely cover input costs. The same potatoes, stored for two months and sold in the lean season, would fetch three times the price.

He knew this. He had always known this. What he did not have was the financing to build cold storage himself, or access to a scheme that would make it economically viable.

Banks Would Not Finance Agri-Infrastructure

Agricultural infrastructure projects occupy an awkward space in the conventional lending framework.

They are too large for microfinance. They are considered too risky - or too unfamiliar - for standard SME loans. The long gestation period before revenue generation makes banks nervous. The absence of traditional collateral among most farmers makes it worse.

The result: infrastructure that was commercially viable on paper could not attract funding in practice. FPOs with genuine aggregation capacity could not build the warehouse. Agri-startups with solid business plans could not construct the processing unit. The bankability gap was not a function of bad projects - it was a function of a financial system not designed for this asset class.

The Fragmentation Problem

Even where infrastructure existed, it was often too far away, too small, or operated by intermediaries who captured most of the value chain margin.

A farmer who had to transport produce 150 kilometres to reach a processing facility was not really accessing infrastructure - they were absorbing transportation costs, quality loss in transit, and intermediary margins that consumed whatever price premium the facility might have offered.

Real infrastructure value requires proximity to the farm gate. And proximity requires distributed, local infrastructure creation - exactly what AIF is designed to enable.

Agri-Startups Were Building in a Vacuum

A new generation of agri-entrepreneurs and startups emerged in the 2010s - people who understood both technology and agriculture, who could see the value chain opportunities clearly, and who wanted to build scalable solutions in cold chain, logistics, processing, and direct-to-market platforms.

Many of them could not access the capital to begin. Commercial bank loans for agricultural infrastructure were difficult to structure. Venture capital was largely uninterested in asset-heavy agri-infra plays. Government schemes were either too small (microfinance) or too large and complex (major national projects).

The middle ground - the ₹50 lakh to ₹5 crore range where most viable local infrastructure projects live - was largely unfunded.

After AIF: How the Scheme Is Rebuilding the Agricultural Value Chain

The Interest Subvention Changes the Math

Consider an agri-entrepreneur who wants to build a cold storage unit for ₹1.5 crore in a semi-urban area of Gujarat.

Without AIF:

Bank loan at 12% per annum

Annual interest: ₹18 lakh

Gestation period before revenue: 12–18 months

Risk: high, bankability: difficult

With AIF:

Bank loan at effectively 9% (3% subvention applied)

Annual interest: ₹13.5 lakh

Credit guarantee covers risk up to ₹2 crore - government pays the fee

Convergence with state schemes possible to reduce equity contribution

The annual saving of ₹4.5 lakh in interest, compounded over 7 years, fundamentally changes the project's viability. Projects that were marginally viable become comfortably bankable. Projects that were not viable at all become feasible with the right structuring.

Farmer Producer Organisations Are Getting Infrastructure They Could Never Afford

FPOs - the farmer collectives that have emerged as a crucial institution in Indian agriculture - face a structural challenge: their members are small and marginal farmers, their balance sheets are thin, and their ability to raise commercial capital is limited despite their collective strength.

AIF specifically addresses this through preferential credit guarantee coverage (via NABSanrakshan for FPOs beyond CGTMSE limits) and through the removal of the 25-project cap for FPO federations.

An FPO in Maharashtra that aggregates produce from 500 farmer members can now realistically plan and finance a pack house and pre-cooling unit at the collection point - reducing post-harvest losses for every member, improving the collective's price realisation, and building a permanent asset that serves the community.

Real Project Scenarios

The Cold Chain Entrepreneur: A young agri-entrepreneur from rural Gujarat identifies a cluster of vegetable farmers with no cold storage access within 50 kilometres. She sets up a small cold storage unit under AIF - ₹90 lakh project, ₹2 crore bank loan availed with 3% interest subvention and CGTMSE guarantee. Within two seasons, vegetable farmers in the cluster see 40% less post-harvest loss. She earns storage revenue. The farmers earn better prices. Both win.

The Processing Cooperative: A PACS (Primary Agricultural Credit Society) in Rajasthan decides to set up a grain processing and storage facility to serve its member farmers. Under AIF, the project is eligible for interest subvention and can converge with state government capital subsidy - reducing the cooperative's equity contribution significantly. The facility now allows member farmers to store grain rather than distress-sell immediately after harvest.

The Agri-Startup: A technology-enabled agri-startup wants to build a network of small pack houses and sorting units across a fruit-growing district in Himachal Pradesh. With the 25-location limit per private entity, they can access AIF funding across multiple sites simultaneously - building scale while keeping each unit financially manageable.

The Solar-Agri Convergence: Post the 2024 expansion, an FPO in Punjab integrates PM-KUSUM Component-A solar infrastructure with their cold storage project under AIF - reducing electricity costs (a major operational expense for cold chain) and making the entire project more financially sustainable.

Why Awareness Remains Low - And Why That Is a Serious Problem

The AIF portal shows 1,73,298 registered beneficiaries across 35 states and UTs. Impressive numbers - but when you consider that India has over 14 crore farm holdings, over 10,000 registered FPOs, and thousands of agri-startups and cooperatives, the penetration of this scheme is still far below its potential.

Why?

Complex eligibility language: Terms like "post-harvest management infrastructure," "community farming assets," and "CGTMSE coverage" are not intuitive for a farmer or a first-generation agri-entrepreneur. The scheme communicates in policy language rather than business language.

Project preparation barriers: AIF requires a viable project report - a document demonstrating technical soundness, financial feasibility, and employment or value-chain impact. Most eligible applicants do not know how to prepare one that meets bank standards.

Bank-level unfamiliarity: Not every branch manager at every participating bank is equally familiar with AIF structuring. Applications that are not well-prepared or well-presented often stall at the bank level - not due to ineligibility, but due to gaps in documentation or project articulation.

Convergence complexity: While convergence with other schemes is a strength of AIF, it is also a source of confusion. Understanding which schemes can be combined, how capital subsidy counts toward promoter contribution, and how to structure the overall financing package requires expertise that most applicants do not have.

Geography and awareness gaps: The scheme's reach in remote and tribal agricultural areas remains limited, despite the explicit design for rural infrastructure. Information simply does not travel as fast as it needs to.

How Euroasia Business Solutions Helps You Access AIF

At Euroasia Business Solutions, we work with farmers, FPOs, cooperatives, agri-entrepreneurs, and startups who want to build agricultural infrastructure - and need structured, expert support to access the financing that makes it viable.

Our AIF support covers:

Project Feasibility Assessment: Before any application, we evaluate your proposed project for AIF eligibility - project type, location, entity category, and financing structure. We identify the optimal approach and flag any issues early.

Project Report Preparation: The project report is the foundation of your AIF application. We prepare technically sound, financially realistic reports that accurately represent your project's viability - meeting bank standards and satisfying AIF guidelines without exaggeration or gap.

Scheme Convergence Structuring: We identify which central and state schemes can be converged with your AIF application, structuring your financing to maximise benefits and minimise equity contribution.

Bank and Lending Institution Coordination: We work with participating lending institutions to ensure your application is correctly filed, completely documented, and actively followed up at every stage - from application to sanction to disbursement.

CGTMSE and NABSanrakshan Guarantee Processing: We handle the credit guarantee paperwork so you receive the collateral-free benefit the scheme is designed to provide.

Post-Disbursement Compliance: AIF loans come with reporting obligations and interest subvention claim processes. We ensure you meet these consistently - protecting your subvention and maintaining your standing with the lending institution.

We do not promise outcomes that depend on government decisions. We ensure that when you are eligible, your application is the strongest it can possibly be.

The Bigger Picture: Why AIF Matters for India's Agricultural Future

India's agricultural challenge is not production. It is value retention.

We grow the food. We just lose too much of it between the farm and the table. And the farmers - who did all the work - absorb most of that loss.

As of August 2024, ₹47,575 crore has been sanctioned for 74,508 projects under AIF, mobilising total investment of ₹78,596 crore in the agriculture sector. This is infrastructure being built. Cold chains being activated. Processing units coming online. Farmers gaining access to facilities that were previously 100 kilometres away.

The 2024 Cabinet expansion made the scheme more comprehensive - all eligible beneficiaries can now create infrastructure for viable community farming assets, the scheme now includes integrated primary and secondary processing projects, and PM-KUSUM Component-A can converge with AIF for farmers, FPOs, cooperatives, and panchayats.

Every cold storage unit built under AIF means less food wasted. Every pack house means better prices for farmers. Every processing facility means more value captured within the agricultural community rather than lost to intermediaries.

This is not just economic policy. It is the structural work of building an agricultural economy that actually works for the people who feed the country.

What You Should Do Next

If you are a farmer, FPO, cooperative, agri-entrepreneur, or startup with a post-harvest infrastructure project in mind - the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund may be exactly the financing mechanism you have been looking for.

The interest subvention, credit guarantee coverage, convergence flexibility, and broad eligibility make AIF one of the most powerful agri-infrastructure financing tools available in India today.

# Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)

Agriculture Infrastructure | Department of Agriculture, Cooperation & Farmers Welfare

 Introduction 

*   Agriculture Infrastructure Fund offers long term financial assistance for building infrastructure for post-harvest stage.
*   Development of such infrastructure shall also address the vagaries of nature, the regional disparities, development of human resource and realization of full potential of our limited land resource.
*   Investments in logistics infrastructure, farmers will be able to sell in the market with reduced post-harvest losses and a smaller number of intermediaries.

 Eligible Applicants 

*   Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS).
*   Marketing Cooperative Societies.
*   Farmer Producers Organizations (FPOs).
*   Farmers.
*   Self Help Group (SHG)
*   Joint Liability Groups (JLG). 
*   Multipurpose Cooperative Societies. 
*   Agri-entrepreneurs, Startups. 
*   Central/State agency or Local Body sponsored Public-Private Partnership Projects. 

 Additional Information 

*   Improved marketing infrastructure to allow farmers to sell directly to a larger base of consumers and hence, increase value realization for the farmers. 
*   All loans under this financing facility will have interest subvention of 3% per annum up to a limit of Rs. 2 crore. 
*   This subvention will be available for a maximum period of 7 years. 
*   In case of loans beyond Rs.2 crore, then interest subvention will be limited up to 2 crore. The extent and percentage of funding to private entrepreneurs out of the total financing facility may be fixed by the National Monitoring Committee. 
*   Credit guarantee coverage will be available for eligible borrowers from this financing facility under Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme for a loan up to Rs. 2 crore. 

![Image 3: Check Eligibility of Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) - JanSamarth](https://www.jansamarth.in/assets/images/find-perfect-scheme-icon.svg)

### Did you find your perfect scheme ?

If you are fulfilling all required criteria mentioned above you can start your loan application via checking your eligibility

Check Eligibility Download Scheme Document Watch Video

## Frequently Asked Questions

Related to Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) Scheme

**1.**What is AIF? 

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund is a medium - long term debt financing facility for investment in viable projects for post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets through interest subvention and credit guarantee.

**2.** Who can apply for the scheme? 

Following are the eligible beneficiaries who can apply for the scheme:

*   Individuals, group of farmers/ growers 
*   Registered Farmer Producer Organizations, Partnership/ Proprietary firms 
*   Companies, Corporations, NGOs, Self Help Groups (SHGs) 
*   Cooperatives, Cooperative Marketing Federations, Autonomous Bodies of the Government, Local Bodies (excluding Municipal Corporations for storage infrastructure projects) 
*   Panchayats 

State agencies including State Government Departments and autonomous organization / State owned corporations such as:

*   Agricultural Produce Market Committees & marketing Boards 
*   State Warehousing Corporations 
*   State Civil Supplies Corporations etc. 

**3.**What products are covered under the scheme? 

The scheme covers post-harvest management projects like supply chain services including:

*   e-marketing platforms 
*   Warehouse 
*   Silos 
*   Aack-houses
*   Assaying units 
*   Sorting & grading units 
*   Cold chain 
*   Logistics facilities 
*   Primary processing centers 

Ripening chambers and other viable projects for building community farming assets such as:

*   Organic input production 
*   Bio stimulant production units 
*   Infrastructure for smart and precision agriculture 
*   Supply chain infrastructure for clusters of crops including exports clusters etc. 

**4.**What is interest subvention offered? 

All loans up to a limit of Rs. 2 crores under this financing facility will have interest subvention of 3% per annum.

This subvention will be available for a maximum period of 7 years.

In case of loans beyond Rs.2 crores, the interest subvention will be limited up to Rs. 2 crores.

**5.**What is collateral for the scheme? 

Credit guarantee coverage will be available for eligible borrowers from this financing facility under Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) scheme for a loan up to Rs. 2 crores.

The fee for this coverage will be paid by the Government.

In case of FPOs the credit guarantee may be availed from the facility created under FPO promotion scheme of DAC&FW.

**6.**What is Moratorium period for the project under the scheme? 

Moratorium period can be from minimum six months and maximum upto 2 years.

For more FAQs [Click Here](http://megcooperation.gov.in/miscellaneous/FAQs_Agriculture_Infrastructure_Fund.pdf)

## Boosting Agricultural Supply Chains Through Infrastructure Investment

Agriculture plays a central role in India’s economy, employing a large share of the rural workforce. Post-harvest losses and weak storage systems often reduce farmer earnings and market efficiency. To address these gaps, the Government of India launched the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund with a financing facility of ₹1 lakh crore for developing post-harvest management infrastructure and community farming assets.

The programme enables affordable credit for projects such as warehouses, cold chains, and collection centres. Through structured lending support and interest subvention, the initiative promotes private investment and encourages agribusiness entrepreneurs to expand infrastructure that improves agricultural value chains.

## Objectives of the Scheme

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund aims to strengthen agricultural supply chains by supporting long-term investments in infrastructure. Financial institutions provide loans through the AIF loan scheme, while the government offers interest subsidies and guarantee support.

Main objectives:

* Improve post-harvest infrastructure at the farm gate
* Reduce wastage and improve agricultural value realisation
* Encourage private and cooperative investment in rural infrastructure
* Strengthen storage, processing, and logistics networks
* Enable farmers and agribusinesses to access affordable farm infrastructure loan options

These measures help create reliable systems for handling agricultural produce from harvest to market.

## Who Can Apply for the Financing Facility

Various agricultural stakeholders can benefit from the scheme. The goal is to make the farm infrastructure loan accessible to both individual and collective farming entities.

Eligible applicants:

* Individual farmers

* Self-Help Groups (SHGs)
* Joint Liability Groups (JLGs)
* Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)
* Agricultural entrepreneurs and start-ups
* Cooperatives and federations
* Central or state agencies

These entities can access financing through the AIF loan scheme for developing agricultural infrastructure projects.

## Types of Infrastructure Supported

Funding under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund focuses on projects that improve storage, handling, and distribution of farm produce.

Examples of supported infrastructure:

* Warehouses and silos

* Sorting and processing centres

Such investments enable farmers and businesses to secure a farm infrastructure loan for building assets that reduce losses and strengthen agricultural markets. # Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund aims to mobilize a medium - long term debt finances facility for investment in viable projects for post-harvest management Infrastructure and community farming assets through incentives and financial support in order to improve agriculture infrastructure in the country.

**Budget Allocation:** Rs. 1 Lakh Crores

**Operating Period of the scheme:** 2020-21 to 2029-30

**Loan disbursement period:** 2020-21 to 2024-24

### Pattern of Assistance

APEDA Registration Is obligatory for every exporter of agriculture commodities. By obtaining Online APEDA Registration, An Exporter Can:

1. Interest Subvention
   * Interest subvention of 3% per annum
   * Max Loan amount to be covered – Rs. 2 Crore
   * Maximum period 7 Years (including Moratorium Period)
2. Collateral free Credit
   * Max upto Rs. 2 Crores
   * Only for Micro and Small Enterprises

### Components of the Scheme

Agriculture Infrastructure Fund will facilitate setting up and modernization of key elements of the value chain including

1. **Post Harvest Management Projects like:**
   1. Supply chain services including e-marketing platforms
   2. Warehouses
   3. Silos
   4. Pack houses
   5. Assaying units
   6. Sorting & grading units
   7. Cold chains (Milk chilling not included)
   8. Logistics facilities
   9. Primary processing centers
   10. Ripening Chambers

1. **Viable projects for building community farming assets including:**
   1. Organic inputs production
   2. Bio stimulant production units
   3. Infrastructure for smart and precision agriculture.
   4. Projects identified for providing supply chain infrastructure for clusters of crops including export clusters.
   5. Projects promoted by Central/State/Local Governments or their agencies under PPP for building community farming assets or post harvest management projects.

### Eligibility Criteria

* Promoter contribution should be minimum 10% of the project cost.
* Disbursal of funds by lending entities to beneficiaries under this scheme shall be in Aadhaar linked bank account.
* Only for primary processing units

### Who can apply

1. ✔️ Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)
2. ✔️ Marketing Cooperative Societies
3. ✔️ Farmer Producers Organizations(FPOs)
4. ✔️ Self Help Group (SHG)
5. ✔️ Farmers
6. ✔️ Joint Liability Groups (JLG)
7. ✔️ Multipurpose Cooperative Societies
8. ✔️ Agri-entrepreneurs
9. ✔️ Startups
10. ✔️ Central/State agency or Local Body sponsored Public Private Partnership Projects.

### Important to remember

1. The extent and percentage of funding to private entrepreneurs out of the total financing facility may be fixed by the National Monitoring Committee
2. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) will be given priority
3. The Lending Institution should have an MOU with NABARD / DAC & FW
4. No Limit on the Loan amount. But the subsidy is limited to Rs. 2 Crores only. In loans above Rs. Crores, the lending institution has the freedom to fix interest rate and obtain collaterals as per guidelines of the RBI
5. Any grant or subsidy available under any present or future scheme of Central/State government can be availed for projects under this financing facility.
6. All assets created under this financing facility shall be geo tagged.
7. 24% of total grants – in – aid under the scheme should be utilized for SC/ST entrepreneurs (16% for SC and 8% for ST)

If you are planning to invest in the agricultural sector and secure bank funding, the Agricultural Infrastructure Fund (AIF) offers a great opportunity. This fund is specifically designed to assist agriculture-based businesses by providing easy bank loans, interest subsidies, and collateral-free funding. In this blog, we will discuss the recent changes in the fund and how you can take advantage of it.

### What Benefits Does AIF Offer?

Launched in 2020, the Agricultural Infrastructure Fund (AIF) aims to support agriculture-based businesses by providing financial assistance. The key benefits under this fund include:

1. **Easy Bank Loans:** Availability of bank loans for agriculture-based businesses.
2. **3% Interest Subsidy:** An interest subsidy of 3% on loans.
3. **Collateral-Free Loans:** Collateral-free loans of up to ₹2 crore.

Additionally, the Indian government has extended this fund until 31st March 2026. This means if you plan to start any agriculture-based business and take a loan before this date, you can avail the benefits of the AIF.

### Recent Changes in the AIF:

There have been some significant changes in the AIF as of 2024. These changes not only broaden the scope of the fund but also provide more opportunities for businesses to benefit from it.

##### 1. **Coverage of Primary and Secondary Processing:**

Earlier, the AIF only covered *primary processing* of agricultural crops (such as wheat cleaning, storage, sorting, etc.). Now, *secondary processing* has also been included. For example, if you process wheat and then use it to make biscuits or other food products, this will now also be covered under the AIF.

Here are some other examples:

* **Cotton**: Previously, cotton ginning and cleaning were covered. Now, if you make fiber from cotton, it will also be covered under the AIF.
* **Oil**: If you extract oil from oilseeds and also refine it, that business will now be covered under the AIF.

This change is a huge opportunity for farmers and businesses looking to invest in secondary processing, as it adds value to their products and enables them to earn more profits.

##### 2. **Sinking of Central Schemes:**

Now, if there are any central-level subsidy schemes that are applicable to agriculture-based projects, these can also be combined with the AIF. For example, if you are availing the NABARD subsidy for warehousing activities, you can now also benefit from the AIF.

Furthermore, the **PMEGP Scheme (Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Program)**, which covers projects up to ₹50 lakh, is also now integrated with the AIF. This means that you can avail both capital subsidy and interest subsidy under both schemes for agriculture-based projects.

##### 3. **Budget Allocation:**

The total budget for the AIF is ₹1 lakh crore, out of which ₹50,000 crore has already been sanctioned. The remaining ₹50,000 crore is still available for sanctioning. Since the scheme is valid until 31st March 2026, there is approximately 1.5 years left to avail these funds. If you are planning an agriculture-based project, it is advisable to apply for AIF funding as soon as possible before the remaining budget is fully allocated.

### How to Avail the AIF Benefits:

To make the most of the Agricultural Infrastructure Fund, you need to:

* **Get your project approved** under the AIF at the earliest.
* **Prepare your project report** and communicate with banks to secure funding.
* **Understand the necessary documentation** to apply for the subsidy and loan.

Hello everyone, welcome to another episode of to the point program. The topic of discussion is agriculture infrastructure fund. First of all, let's see why this topic is in the news over 1.13 lakh agri projects funded under the agriculture infrastructure fund AIF focusing on enhancing post-h harvest infrastructure and farmer incomes. Now let's discuss what is agriculture infrastructure fund. The agriculture infrastructure fund AIF launched in 202021 aims to enhance posth harvest and farmgate infrastructure to boost productivity, reduce losses and improve market access. It provides debt financing with interestion and credit guarantee for viable projects in storage, logistics and farming infrastructure by developing facilities like warehouses, cold storage and grading units. The AIF helps farmers store produce efficiently, sell at better prices and reduce reliance on intermediaries, ultimately increasing their income. The scheme benefits farmers, agri entrepreneurs, cooperatives and consumers. Now let's discuss about key government initiatives supporting AIF. Integrated coal chain food processing and preservation infrastructure scheme focuses on reducing posth harvest losses and ensuring fair prices for farmers. Capital Investment Subsidy for cold storage offers subsidies for constructing, expanding and modernizing cold stoages for horicultural produce. Agricultural marketing infrastructure AMI strengthens marketing infrastructure promoting better access to markets for rural farmers. Pradhan Mantri Matsi Sampa Yojana PMMSY focuses on fish production, posth harvest infrastructure and job creation across the fisheries value chain. Digital public infrastructure DPI aims to provide seamless digital access to farmers enhancing efficiency and transparency across the agri value chain. Now let's discuss what is posth harvest management. Post-h harvest management refers to the activities and techniques used to preserve and protect crops after they have been harvested. This includes activities such as cleaning, sorting, grading, packaging, storage, and transportation. The goal of posth harvest management is to maintain the quality and safety of the crops as well as to extend their shelf life so that they can be sold and consumed at a later time. The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) is a robust initiative by the Central Government of India, aimed at boosting the agriculture sector through infrastructural support and financial assistance. Launched in 2020 by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmer Welfare, this scheme comes with a significant budget allocation of 1 lakh crore, reflecting the government’s commitment to transforming and modernizing agriculture across India. By covering a broad range of agribusinesses, AIF provides a tremendous opportunity for entrepreneurs, farmers, and agriculture-based business owners to access funding, develop efficient agri-based projects, and scale operations in line with market demands.

# Top 5 Business Sectors Covered by the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

[Download AIF E-Book](https://pages.razorpay.com/agricultureinfrastructurefund)

The **Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF)** is a robust initiative by the Central Government of India, aimed at boosting the agriculture sector through infrastructural support and financial assistance. Launched in 2020 by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmer Welfare, this scheme comes with a significant budget allocation of 1 lakh crore, reflecting the government’s commitment to transforming and modernizing agriculture across India. By covering a broad range of agribusinesses, AIF provides a tremendous opportunity for entrepreneurs, farmers, and agriculture-based business owners to access funding, develop efficient agri-based projects, and scale operations in line with market demands.

In this guide, we will discuss the types of businesses eligible for the AIF scheme, the potential benefits, and the broad applicant eligibility framework.

## 1. Key Sectors Covered Under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

The AIF scheme offers coverage for diverse types of agriculture-based businesses, making it an excellent resource for both traditional and innovative agri-businesses. Here are the key sectors eligible for funding under this scheme:

### (i) E-Marketing Platforms

Businesses launching **e-marketing platforms for agriculture produce** are covered under this scheme. This includes platforms dedicated to selling, distributing, or marketing agri-products. If your business involves the development of digital solutions for agriculture, including market linkage and e-commerce models, you are eligible to apply for AIF benefits.

### (ii) Storage Facilities

Infrastructure such as **cold storage, warehouses, wrapping chambers, and sorting and grading units** are all crucial for the agriculture supply chain. These facilities help in storing fresh produce, ensuring better shelf life, and reducing spoilage. If you are setting up any of these facilities, AIF provides an opportunity for you to avail of financial assistance, helping your business become a reliable asset in post-harvest management.

### (iii) Waste and Residue Management

The AIF scheme also encourages **waste and residue management** in agriculture, an essential aspect of sustainable agriculture. Projects related to biomass energy, such as waste management, biomass briquettes, pellets, and compressed biogas, are covered. Such initiatives not only benefit your business but also support environmental sustainability by repurposing agricultural waste into useful products.

### (iv) Primary Processing Units

For businesses dealing with **primary processing of crops** like rice, cotton, sugarcane, bamboo, jute, fruits, and vegetables, the AIF scheme provides substantial support. Primary processing includes activities such as sorting, grading, washing, and storage, which add value to raw agricultural products. Setting up primary processing units helps streamline the supply chain, improve product quality, and meet consumer demand for value-added products.

### (v) Farming-Based Activities

The scheme includes a variety of **farming-related activities** such as vermicompost production, bee-farming, honey processing, tissue cultures, nurseries, and other horticulture ventures. It also covers any agricultural operations involving equipment for planting, harvesting, or post-harvest handling. This broad scope enables agripreneurs to explore a wide range of opportunities under the AIF.

## 2. Additional Flexibility in the AIF Scheme

One unique feature of the AIF scheme is its **flexibility in accepting new allied businesses** that align with agriculture. The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmer Welfare has not set rigid boundaries for eligibility; if a new agribusiness or allied sector is deemed relevant, it can be considered for funding. This flexibility has helped numerous agripreneurs with innovative business ideas to benefit from AIF, fostering a dynamic ecosystem of agri-based enterprises.

## 3. Who is Eligible to Apply for the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund?

A significant benefit of the AIF is its **inclusive eligibility framework**. If you are involved in agriculture in any of the following capacities, you can apply for the AIF scheme:

* **Individual Entrepreneurs**: Business owners or individuals planning to establish agri-based ventures.
* **Proprietorship Firms**: Firms owned by a single individual but involved in agricultural activities.
* **Partnership Firms and Companies**: Businesses with two or more partners involved in agriculture projects.
* **Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs)**: Registered LLPs engaged in agriculture-based businesses.
* **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**: Organized groups of farmers or agripreneurs working on a joint agriculture project.
* **Start-ups and Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs)**: These groups promote collective farming and ensure that small farmers benefit from shared resources and market access.

With such an inclusive eligibility structure, AIF opens doors for diverse types of agripreneurs, from small farmers to large agribusiness firms.

## 4. Key Benefits of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund Scheme

The AIF scheme provides several advantages to agripreneurs, including:

* **Access to Affordable Loans**: AIF offers loans at subsidized interest rates, making it easier for businesses to access the capital needed for expansion.
* **Structured Ecosystem**: The scheme facilitates a collaborative ecosystem where the government, bankers, farmers, and businesses work together to maximize agriculture sector growth.
* **Enhanced Market Linkage**: By supporting the development of e-marketing platforms and infrastructure, AIF improves farmers’ access to markets.
* **Focus on Sustainability**: Through funding for waste and residue management, the scheme encourages environmentally sustainable practices.
* **Wider Coverage**: The scheme’s flexibility in business coverage allows diverse projects in horticulture, storage management, primary processing, and other allied sectors to benefit from AIF.

## 5. How to Apply for the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund

To apply for the AIF scheme, follow these steps:

1. **Prepare a Project Proposal**: Outline your business objectives, projected costs, and the specific agri-based activities your business will undertake.
2. **Gather Necessary Documents**: Depending on the type of business, prepare necessary documentation such as registration certificates, business plans, and identity proof.
3. **Connect with Financial Institutions**: Public sector banks, NBFCs, private and commercial banks have MoUs with the Ministry of Agriculture for the AIF scheme. Approach these institutions to understand the loan application process.
4. **Complete Online Application**: Submit your project details on the Ministry of Agriculture’s portal for AIF. This may require attaching all relevant documents and filling out necessary information related to your business.
5. **Submit and Track Progress**: Once your application is submitted, stay in touch with your bank to track the loan processing and ensure timely updates.

## Conclusion

The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund is an ambitious initiative that holds tremendous promise for agribusinesses across India. By offering financial support, encouraging market access, and supporting sustainable practices, AIF is helping to transform India’s agriculture sector and increase farmer incomes. If you are involved in or planning to start an agri-based business, the AIF scheme can serve as a valuable resource for growth. Consider exploring this opportunity to scale your business, contribute to the agriculture economy, and participate in the mission to transform India’s agricultural landscape.

# Shantanu Pendsey’s Post

[Shantanu Pendsey](https://in.linkedin.com/in/shantanu-pendsey-99487546?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Fshantanu-pendsey-99487546_agriculture-infrastructure-fund-aif-activity-7271060510966456320-ft_V&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

“Agriculture Infrastructure Fund” (AIF): A Game Changer in Transforming Agriculture and Enhancing Farmers’ Income The AIF, a visionary initiative of the Indian Govt in 2020, addresses critical challenges in agriculture by enhancing infrastructure across the value chain. Farmers, who bear the highest risks, often receive minimal rewards due to their limited role in the supply chain. India also faces annual post-harvest losses exceeding ₹1.50 trillion. AIF aims at providing financial support for infrastructure development, including secondary processing integrated projects to maximise its impact and empowering farmers to become part of supply chain. Key Features - 1. Funding Mechanism: The loans are collateral free Upto ₹2 crores with an effective rate of interest of just 6% p.a. (net of interest subvention) with repayment period up to 7 years and moratorium upto 2 years. 2. Eligible Beneficiaries: Farmers, FPOs, PACS, Startups, Agri-entrepreneurs, Coop Institutions, and Public-Private partnerships. 3. Focus Areas: Post-harvest infrastructure: warehouses, cold chains, logistics, and silos. Community farming assets: farm gates, ripening chambers, and sorting units. Secondary processing: food processing, value addition, packaging, and marketing. Addressing Key Agricultural Challenges 1. Post-Harvest Infrastructure: Mitigates 15-20% post-harvest losses via modern storage and transportation. Enhances price realization by allowing farmers to store and sell produce at optimal times. 2. Market Linkages: Facilitates direct farmer access to consumers, retailers, and exporters, reducing intermediaries. Infrastructure support for e-NAM ensures competitive pricing and online trading. Empowers FPOs and cooperatives to set up shared infrastructure, promoting economies of scale. Secondary Processing: A Transformative Inclusion 1. Higher Margins: Farmers gain a greater share of final product value. Expands export opportunities for processed goods, fetching premium prices. 2. Income Diversification: Farmers mitigate risks by investing in processing units for multiple products. The Way Forward 1. Integrated Value Chain Projects: Clusters based approach. Partnerships with private players. 2. Technology Adoption: IoT-enabled cold chains with traceability and mobile apps for farmer-market engagement. 3. Skill Development: Training and promotion for awareness. The Impact Since inception of AIF, a sum of Rs. 51783 Crs has been sanctioned by the Banks for 85,314 Agri Infra projects with total investment flow of Rs. 85,208 Crs in improving the farm gate infrastructure which is stupendous progress. AIF is, thus, a transformative initiative aimed at addressing systemic inefficiencies in Indian agricultural sector by ensuring higher income for farmers and creating a resilient and sustainable supply chain. The AIF can realise the vision of “Atmanirbhar Bharat” and secure a prosperous future for Indian farmers.

Key Challenges: \* Water Scarcity: Reliance on the Nile River and increasing water demand pose the most critical long-term challenge, exacerbated by upstream developments and climate change. \* Climate Change: Rising temperatures and extreme weather threaten crop yields and require significant adaptation efforts. \* Urban Encroachment: The loss of fertile land in the Nile Delta to urbanization is a persistent problem. \* Fragmented Land Holdings: The dominance of small farms often using traditional practices can hinder the adoption of modern, high-cost technologies. In summary, the future of Egyptian agriculture is one of strategic transformation, leveraging technology and major government projects to overcome resource constraints and climate vulnerabilities.

  Reframing Malawi’s Maize Crisis: A Strategic Perspective Malawi’s agricultural sector is the backbone of its economy. Approximately 80% of the population (~16 million people), depend on agriculture. Furthermore, over 80% of the labour force, (~6.4 million people) are engaged in agricultural activities. 59% of Malawi’s land is suitable for farming, and 38% is classified as arable. Malawi also has abundant freshwater resources, including Lake Malawi, which covers about 20–23.6% of the country’s area, and rivers such as the Shire, Ruo, Bua, and Dwangwa. These water bodies collectively represent 16.14 billion cubic meters of freshwater. Assuming total efficient utilization of arable land for maize production, Malawi could produce 24 million tonnes of maize in one cycle using the rainy season alone. With irrigation and two production cycles per year, this figure could double to 48 million tonnes annually. In comparison, the country’s estimated maize consumption in 2024 was just 3.5 million tonnes. Currently, Malawi cultivates 1.7 million hectares of land for maize. If this land were used efficiently, a single cycle could yield 20.4 million tonnes, and with irrigation, 40.8 million tonnes annually. Even when factoring in a 50% variance to account for inefficiencies and land allocated to other crops, the country could still produce 20 million tonnes annually—8.5 times the national consumption, including industrial use. Despite this potential, Malawi only produced approximately 2.9 million tonnes in 2024/25, resulting in a deficit of 600,000 tonnes. To address this, 200,000 tonnes will be imported from Zambia, and the government plans to spend MWK 370 billion (USD 21 million) on maize procurement. A hectare of maize production costs around MWK 480,000 (Min), yielding 2 tonnes inefficiently or 6 tonnes efficiently. With MWK 370 billion, Malawi could fund 770,833 hectares, producing 1.54 million tonnes at inefficient yield or 4.63 million tonnes at efficient yield. The key takeaway is that efficient use of resources and modern agricultural practices, including irrigation, even on the existing 1.7 million hectares, could result in a surplus of over 1 million tonnes annually. Expanding land use and irrigation could double this surplus, enable exports and help to ease Malawi’s foreign exchange shortages. This scenario focuses solely on maize. Incorporating soya and other cash crops, along with land expansion, could position Malawi for agricultural surplus and export growth. In essence, Malawi need not be in a food crisis. With the right investments in agriculture, the country can achieve food security and export-driven growth. While the government plays a pivotal role, citizens must also embrace commercial farming for export. A restructured fiscal budget over the next five years, prioritizing agriculture investment and not subsidy programs, could transform Malawi’s agricultural and economic future.

  🌿 Xeriscaping in Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) 🌍 Xeriscaping represents an innovative water-efficient approach that supports climate-smart agriculture by integrating sustainable land use, soil care, and adaptive crop management. Derived from the Greek word “xeros” meaning “dry,” xeriscaping focuses on minimizing water dependency while sustaining productivity in drought-prone and semi-arid regions. 🌱 Concept Overview Xeriscaping in CSA combines ecological landscape design with water-efficient agricultural practices to ensure long-term resource conservation. It involves planning crop zones based on water needs, improving soil with organic matter and biochar, and selecting drought-resilient plants. The objective is to create a self-sustaining ecosystem that conserves soil moisture, enhances fertility, and reduces irrigation costs. 💧 Benefits in the CSA Context 1️⃣ Water Conservation – Reduces irrigation demand through drought-tolerant species and efficient water management. 2️⃣ Carbon Mitigation – Enhances soil carbon sequestration via biochar and organic mulching. 3️⃣ Climate Resilience – Strengthens soil health, reduces erosion, and stabilizes crop yields under variable climates. 4️⃣ Economic Efficiency – Minimizes input costs by lowering water and energy use, benefiting smallholders. 🔑 Key Principles of Xeriscaping in CSA 1. Smart Planning & Design: Strategic zoning based on crop water needs, slope, and sunlight. 2. Soil Improvement: Organic matter and biochar addition to increase water-holding capacity and microbial activity. 3. Drought-Resilient Plant Selection: Use of native, deep-rooted, and climate-adapted varieties that need minimal irrigation. 4. Efficient Irrigation Systems: Adoption of drip, sprinkler, or subsurface irrigation for precision water use. 5. Mulching & Ground Cover: Applying organic or biodegradable mulch to reduce evaporation and suppress weeds. 6. Water Harvesting & Recycling: Collecting rainwater, reusing greywater, and improving watershed management. 7. Maintenance & Monitoring: Employing remote sensing and soil-moisture sensors to ensure sustainability. 🌎 Global & Indian Examples • United States (Colorado, Arizona): Urban xeriscaping has reduced water use by 50%. • Israel: Integrated reclaimed water and advanced drip irrigation systems. • India (Rajasthan, Gujarat): Adoption of millet-based, dryland cropping systems adapted to arid conditions. These examples highlight policy support and innovation gaps that need adoption in developing regions. ⚙️ Integration with Modern CSA Technologies • GIS Mapping & Remote Sensing • AI-based Crop Selection • Solar-Powered Irrigation • Policy & Subsidy Support. 🌾 Conclusion Xeriscaping in CSA represents a transformative step toward sustainable, low-carbon, and water-smart agriculture. It builds resilience to drought, enhances biodiversity, and aligns perfectly with the goals of sustainable land and water management in an era of climate uncertainty.

| Interest Subvention | 3% per annum for limit up to Rs.2.00cr for a maximum period of 7 years |
| Processing charges | Up to Rs. 50,000/- - Nil  Above Rs. 50,000/- **-** 0.25% of the limit sanctioned + applicable GST. |
|  | Repayment period | Maximum 12 years including holiday period |
| Holiday period | Maximum 24 Months |

results.title: National Agriculture Infra Financing Facility
results.content:
Size of the financing facility – ₹ 1 lakh Crore.

Credit Guarantee for loans up to ₹ 2 Crore.

Interest subvention of 3% p.a., limited to ₹ 2 crore per project in one location, though loan amount can be higher.

Cap on lending rate, so that benefit of interest subsidy reaches the beneficiary and services to farmers remain affordable.

Multiple lending institutions including Commercial Banks, Cooperative Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, NCDC, NBFCs etc.

One eligible entity puts up projects in different locations then all such projects will be eligible under the scheme for loan upto ₹ 2 crore.

For a private sector entity, such as farmer, agri entrepreneur, start-up there will be a limit of maximum of 25 such projects. [...] Agriculture Infrastructure Financing Facility

The role of infrastructure is crucial for agriculture development and
for taking the production dynamics to the next level. It is only
through the development of infrastructure, especially at the post
harvest stage that the produce can be optimally utilized with
opportunity for value addition and fair deal for the farmers.
Development of such infrastructure shall also address the vagaries of
nature, the regional disparities, development of human resource and
realization of full potential of our limited land resource.

opportunity for value addition and fair deal for the farmers.
Development of such infrastructure shall also address the vagaries of
nature, the regional disparities, development of human resource and
realization of full potential of our limited land resource.

**Project Management Unit to provide** handholding support for projects including project preparation.

**Size of the financing facility –** ₹ 1 lakh Crore.

**Credit Guarantee for loans** up to ₹ 2 Crore.

**Interest subvention of 3% p.a.,** limited to ₹ 2 crore per project in one location, though loan amount can be higher.

**Cap on lending rate, so that benefit** of interest subsidy reaches the beneficiary and services to farmers remain affordable.

**Multiple lending institutions including** Commercial Banks, Cooperative Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, NCDC, NBFCs etc.

**One eligible entity puts up projects in** different locations then all such projects will be eligible under the scheme for loan upto ₹ 2 crore.

**For a private sector entity, such as farmer,** agri entrepreneur, start-up there will be a limit of maximum of 25 such projects.
